tldr: Extremely large policy gradients obtained by backpropagating through a learned world model are mostly spurious signals that fail to hold in the simulator. Capping gradient norms at the rollout level dramatically improves a humanoid's motion tracking performance on unseen motions and speeds up training.

The green translucent model indicates the reference motion. In the sit-down motion with hands on the ground (top), the baseline falls midway, whereas the proposed method maintains its posture to the end. In intense hip-hop dance (bottom), the proposed method keeps tracking errors significantly smaller.
overview:
Humanoid motion tracking, which trains a humanoid robot to mimic massive motion capture datasets, is a foundational technology for teleoperation and motion generation. Recently, methods such as SuperMimic have trained a neural "world model" to emulate robot dynamics and backpropagated reward gradients directly into the policy through imagined trajectories. This achieves dramatic training speedups compared to traditional model-free reinforcement learning.

However, just like differentiable simulation, it suffers from a fundamental issue: even if model predictions are accurate, their derivatives (gradients) may not be. The authors thoroughly examined how much the gradients computed by a learned world model actually hold in the physical simulator. The findings were striking: the top $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet when actions are moved along these directions in the simulator, only $1\%$ of the predicted return change is realized.

Based on this insight, the authors introduced three improvements. First, capping each rollout's action-gradient norm at $10$ times the batch median. Second, drawing imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm to reduce what gets removed by the cap. Third, having the world model and critic predict where the policy will fail across all clips, resetting episodes at those challenging points.

Evaluated on a Unitree G1 humanoid across 353 unseen motions not performed by any actor during training, this approach raised normalized return from $0.953$ to $0.967$ and halved persistently falling test clips. Furthermore, it reached the baseline's final performance in just $40\%$ of the iterations and half the training time.
contributions: Demonstrated through duplicate-rollout tests and simulator perturbation tests that world-model policy gradients stop holding in the simulator once they exceed a few times the batch median.
Proposed an adaptive, hyperparameter-robust gradient capping method that bounds each rollout's action-gradient norm at a constant multiple (10x) of the batch median.
Introduced a model-ranked reset mechanism that identifies failure-prone motion frames across the entire dataset using world model and critic predictions alone, without running the actual environment.
Constructed a strict generalization benchmark using completely unseen actors and motions, proving higher tracking accuracy and halving training time for humanoid tracking.

sections.heading: How much can we trust world model gradients?
sections.summary: Updating policies by differentiating through world models is fast, but extreme gradients tend to hijack the updates. Experiments revealed that gradients exceeding a few times the median are virtually noise in the simulator, motivating a principled capping strategy.
sections.details:
Building a generalist motion tracker that enables humanoid robots to mimic arbitrary human movement is a bedrock for whole-body control. However, training model-free reinforcement learning across hundreds of hours of motion requires clusters of GPUs computing for days.

In response, first-order gradient methods like SuperMimic have emerged. They learn a world model approximating transition dynamics and backpropagate returns across time, delivering strong tracking on a single GPU in just hours. However, differentiating through contact-rich physics carries severe risks of exploding or misdirected gradients.

Examining trained models closely reveals that rollouts whose gradient norm exceeds $30$ times the batch median make up only $0.5\%$ of all rollouts. Yet that tiny $0.5\%$ accounts for $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm and $99\%$ of the sum of squared norms. Policy updates are essentially hijacked by a handful of extreme outliers.

To see if these massive gradients carry real signal, the authors ran two tests: rolling out a second time from the exact same state under independent noise, and applying gradient perturbations directly in the physical simulator. In both tests, gradients beyond a few times the median were entirely unconfirmed. Above $30$ times the median, the simulator delivered only $1\%$ of the return improvement predicted by the model.

The takeaway is straightforward: credible gradient information plateaus at a small multiple of the median, meaning gradient norms should be capped per rollout. Pairing this cap with importance sampling of high-gradient start states and model-guided episode resets yielded superior tracking on unseen motions alongside a greater than $2\times$ training speedup.

sections.heading: The evolution of large-scale tracking and first-order gradients
sections.summary: Physics-based motion tracking has shifted from model-free RL to differentiable models. This work bridges theoretical and empirical treatments of exploding gradients while introducing a model-driven curriculum that pinpoints hard frames without past visitation history.
sections.details:
### Advances in Large-Scale Motion Tracking
Since DeepMimic, physical tracking frameworks have relied on random state initialization and early termination upon falling. The key to scaling datasets is deciding where episodes should start. Frameworks like PHC, BeyondMimic, SONIC, and SuperMimic record clips and time bins where the robot previously fell or failed, upweighting sampling probabilities for those failure bins. However, these methods depend on empirical visitation history. This paper differentiates itself by using the world model and critic to score difficulty across the entire motion library without running the robot in the simulator.

### First-Order Policy Gradients and Clipping
Differentiating simulators or learned models produces low-variance gradients, but chaotic dynamics and contacts frequently generate numerical outliers. Prior work typically mitigated this by shortening rollout horizons or clipping the batch gradient norm. The per-sample quantile clipping used here mirrors the mathematical machinery of differentially private SGD (DP-SGD). In this work, it is adopted not for privacy, but to preserve physical validity in gradients.

### Gradient-Norm Sampling and Concurrent Work
Sampling proportional to a sample's gradient norm and weighting by its inverse is known as optimal importance sampling in SGD. This work adapts that concept to choose imagination start states. Concurrently, \nabla Mimic highlighted heavy-tailed gradients in humanoid tracking and clipped them at each backpropagation step. In contrast, this paper evaluates validity across the entire trajectory and applies capping at the rollout level.

sections.heading: Foundations of world-model-based motion tracking
sections.summary: A review of the SuperMimic baseline: three core components—a policy outputting joint targets, a world model predicting transitions, and a critic estimating cumulative returns—train collaboratively.
sections.details:
### III-A Motion Tracking with World Models
The platform is the Unitree G1 humanoid. The simulator is Newton (a MuJoCo Warp solver), running physics at 200 Hz and joint position control at 50 Hz. The task is to track reference motion-capture frame sequences with each link of the robot.
The policy $\pi_\theta$ receives a 10-step history of proprioceptive states (joint positions and velocities) and 10 future reference poses, outputting target joint positions $a_t$. The world model $f_\omega$ predicts the next state from the current state and action, trained on a replay buffer gathered from parallel simulation. The reward function combines exponential kernels penalizing link position, orientation, and velocity errors with action penalties. Performance is measured by normalized return (1.0 maximum), which divides cumulative reward by episode length.

### III-B Computing First-Order Policy Gradients
At each training iteration, $B$ states are sampled from the replay buffer, and the policy is rolled out for $H$ steps inside the world model (imagination). Multiplying survival probabilities $c_t$ derived from model states and bootstrapping terminal values with the critic $V_\psi$ yields the objective $J_b$.
The policy parameters $\theta$ are updated using gradients backpropagated through this $H$-step unroll. Defining the total derivative with respect to action at step $t$ as $g_{b,t} = \mathrm{d}J_b / \mathrm{d}a_{b,t}$, the rollout gradient norm is $G_b = (\sum_t \|g_{b,t}\|^2)^{1/2}$. This norm $G_b$ is the primary subject of investigation.

### III-C Resetting Episodes
When the robot falls or reaches a clip's end, the episode resets to a frame in the library. SuperMimic divides motion clips into roughly 1-second bins, tracks returns when initialized from each bin, and resets to failure-prone bins with a $40\%$ probability.

sections.heading: How much of the model's gradient is real?
sections.summary: Two validation tests on trained models reveal that massive policy gradients exceeding a few times the batch median are vulnerable to noise and deliver almost no return improvement in the simulator, acting as spurious signals.
sections.details:
### IV-A A Tiny Fraction of Rollouts Dominates Gradients
Analyzing 65,536 imagined rollouts with horizon $H=64$, $88\%$ exhibited gradient norms $G_b$ below $3$ times the batch median. Extreme rollouts exceeding $30$ times the median made up just $0.45\%$. Yet this $0.45\%$ accounted for $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm and $99\%$ of the sum of squared norms. Unweighted batch averaging allows a tiny fraction of outliers to dominate the policy update.

### IV-B Test 1: Does a Second Rollout from the Same State Agree?
Imagination is deterministic except for observation noise fed into the policy. When rolling out twice from the exact same starting state under independent observation noise, the correlation between resulting gradients $g$ and $g'$ tells a clear story. Below $3$ times the median, over $80\%$ of the norm is reproduced. Between $5$ and $30$ times the median, the reproducible component plateaus at around $3$ to $4$ times the median regardless of how large the norm grows. Beyond $30$ times, the gradients scatter like random noise.

### IV-C Test 2: Does Stepping Along the Gradient Improve Simulator Return?
Next, actions in the simulator were perturbed along the model's gradient direction to measure how much of the predicted return change actually occurs in simulation (Trust).
The contrast was stark. For rollouts with gradient norms below the median, the simulator delivered $94\%$ of the model's predicted gain. Between $3$ and $10$ times the median, this dropped to $48\%$; between $10$ and $30$ times, to $12\%$; and above $30$ times, to a mere $1\%$. Comparing with the model's own finite differences showed that while the model remains smooth between $3$ and $10$ times the median, it diverges from simulator physics. Above $10$ times, the model's local gradients break down entirely.

### IV-D Conclusion: Capping at a Multiple of the Median is Rational
Both tests point to the same conclusion: useful gradient information saturates at $\min(G, k \cdot \operatorname{med} G)$. Using gradients unconstrained wastes updates on noise, while normalizing every rollout to unit length discards legitimate signal variations between $0.3$ and $3$ times the median. The authors selected $k=10$ as the sweet spot to filter noise while preserving valid learning signal.

sections.heading: Gradient capping, smarter sampling, and model-ranked resets
sections.summary: Three upgrades are made to SuperMimic: rollout-level adaptive gradient capping, gradient-norm importance sampling for imagination start states, and fast model-based reset ranking across the full dataset.
sections.details:
### V-A Rollout-Level Adaptive Gradient Capping
Using each rollout's action-gradient norm $G_b$ and the batch median $\operatorname{med} G$, a per-rollout weight $w_b = \min(1, 10 \cdot \operatorname{med} G / G_b)$ is computed. Parameters are updated via the weighted average $\frac{1}{B} \sum_b w_b \nabla_\theta J_b$. Because the cap is scaled relative to the batch median, it requires no manual hyperparameter tuning as rewards shift or training progresses.
In implementation, a zero dummy tensor is added to each action step during the model backward pass to compute $G_b$ and determine $w_b$. A second pass weights the cached policy outputs before backpropagating into policy parameters. Because capping suppresses gradient explosion, the imagination horizon $H$ can be safely doubled from 32 to 64 steps, enabling updates based on longer-term dynamics.

### V-B Start State Sampling by Gradient Norm (Start Draw)
Because capping trims large gradients, states prone to high gradient norms risk being under-represented. To counter this, states expected to produce larger gradients are drawn with higher probability $q(s)$ and weighted by $1/q$ during loss computation. This importance sampling reduces what gets clipped while preserving unbiased expectations. Concretely, states are partitioned into 32 critic-value bins, referencing historical running averages of gradient norms to assign sampling probabilities.

### V-C Model-Ranked Difficulty Resets
The conventional strategy of recording visited failure bins requires vast time to cover hundreds of thousands of bins. Instead, every 2,000 iterations, the policy is unrolled for 32 steps in the world model from every reference bin in the library, scoring each via the critic. The lowest $5\%$ of bins by predicted return are designated as the "Hard set," receiving $40\%$ of all episode resets. Scoring all 740,000 bins takes roughly 30 seconds, adding just $3\%$ to overall training time for an efficient curriculum.

sections.heading: Empirical results: Generalization to unseen motions and faster training
sections.summary: Evaluated on a Unitree G1 with 353 unseen test motions, the proposed method substantially increased tracking returns, halved persistent falls, and matched baseline final returns in half the time and 40% of the iterations.
sections.details:
### VI-A Experimental Setup
The benchmark uses the BONES-SEED dataset (around 223 hours, 109k clips) retargeted to the Unitree G1. Crucially, the train/test split is partitioned by distinct motions rather than actors. The 353 test motions (11,828 clips, 21.3 hours) were never performed by any training actor. Metrics include mean normalized return, bottom-$10\%$ and bottom-$1\%$ return tails, and the count of persistently falling clips at the end of episodes.

### VI-B Core Results and Training Speed
On the 29-DoF Unitree G1, test return on unseen motions rose from SuperMimic's 0.9531 to 0.9671 (eliminating $30\%$ of remaining tracking error). Gains were most pronounced on challenging motions: bottom-$10\%$ clip returns jumped by +0.076, bottom-$1\%$ returns rose from 0.65 to 0.76, and persistently failing clips were halved from 15–18 to 7–10.
Training efficiency was equally notable: the proposed method surpassed the baseline's 25,000-iteration final return (approx. 2.5 hours) in around 10,000 iterations (approx. 1.2 hours).

### VI-C Component Ablations
Ablation studies isolated the contributions of each piece:
- **Gradient Capping**: The primary driver of mean return gains. Without it, lengthening the horizon to 64 degrades performance due to accumulated gradient noise.
- **Model-Ranked Resets**: The primary driver of tail improvements, substantially lifting the bottom-$10\%$ return and cutting falling clips.
- **Start State Sampling**: Provides modest improvements when paired with model resets, but when tested alongside baseline resets, it reduced falling clips from 43 to 2.

### VI-D Cross-Robot and Cross-Dataset Validation
On a 23-DoF G1, test returns rose from 0.9648 to 0.9746, reaching baseline performance in 0.94 hours. On the standard LAFAN1 benchmark (evaluated on the same clips as prior work), return improved from 0.9061 to 0.9347, showing marked progress on difficult motions such as rising from the ground.

sections.heading: Limitations: Hardware torque bounds and computation overhead
sections.summary: Analysis of persistent failures reveals motion capture data demanding torques far exceeding the robot's physical motor limits. Additionally, the extra backward pass for gradient capping modestly increases per-iteration runtime.
sections.details:
### Motions Exceeding Actuator Limits
Even with the proposed method, five test clips failed persistently across all three random seeds (e.g., handstands and burpees). Inverse dynamics analysis showed these motions demand up to 5.8 times the Unitree G1 wrist motor torque limit (5 Nm), exceeding limits across $74\%$ of frames. Rather than an algorithmic failure, these motions are physically impossible for the hardware. This highlights the need for torque-limit filtering during motion preprocessing.

### Computational Overhead and Parameter Choice
Computing rollout gradient norms before weighting requires two policy forward-backward passes, increasing per-iteration time by roughly $22\%$ (optimizable via CUDA graph capture). Furthermore, while capping at 10 times the median proved empirically robust across experiments, the threshold lacks a rigorous mathematical derivation for its optimal value.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Trusting what repeats drives tracking breakthroughs
sections.summary: Questioning the reproducibility of world model policy gradients and trusting only the validated band via capping achieved substantial gains in tracking performance and training speed for humanoid robots.
sections.details:
Through careful empirical testing, this study revealed that policy gradients obtained from learned world models are heavily corrupted by rare, massive outliers. By establishing a straightforward capping rule based on simulator reproducibility and coupling it with model-driven reset ranking, the proposed approach overcomes key limitations of existing trackers.

These insights extend well beyond humanoid tracking, offering immediate practical guidelines for reinforcement learning and robotic control paradigms that optimize policies through learned world models or differentiable simulators.

sections.heading: Appendix: Model-ranked reset analysis and difficulty scoring
sections.summary: Supplementary details examining score distributions across 740k motion bins, the sparse visitation issue in baseline trackers, and model detection accuracy for failure bins.
sections.details:
### Superiority of Model-Predicted Resets
In the baseline method, $75\%$ of the 746,000 motion bins are visited only once or twice across all 25,000 training iterations. Estimating true bin difficulty from such sparse data is statistically unreliable.
In contrast, the proposed method rolls out the world model from reference poses across all bins to compute 32-step predicted returns. Without running the simulator, it accurately identifies the hardest $5\%$ of bins in the entire library. When evaluating ROC AUC for detecting the hardest bins that actually fail in simulation on test motions, the critic alone achieves 0.74–0.77, whereas the world-model-unrolled return achieves an outstanding 0.91–0.92.

captions.F9: Mechanism of model-ranked difficulty resets. (a) Predicted returns across motion bins for each clip (darker bins represent the hardest 5%). (b) Under baseline resets, 75% of bins are visited only 1–2 times during training, yielding noisy scores. (c) Proposed model-predicted returns (blue) predict bins that actually fail in simulation with far greater precision than the critic alone (gray).

takeaways: Massive policy gradients from world models (exceeding a few times the batch median) do not hold in the simulator; they act as noise and should be capped.
Gradient capping should be applied at the rollout level using a relative threshold against the batch median (e.g., 10x), ensuring robust training without manual hyperparameter tuning.
Unrolling the world model across the motion library identifies difficult motions rapidly and accurately without environment execution, enabling targeted curriculum resets.
Bounding model gradients to their trustworthy regime allows doubling the imagination horizon, producing more stable, long-horizon control policies.
limitations: No learning method can prevent falls on motion capture data that grossly exceeds the robot's physical actuator torque limits (such as wrist limits during handstands).
Computing gradient norms per rollout requires two policy passes, increasing per-iteration computation time by approximately 22%.
The capping threshold of 10 times the median was determined empirically; a mathematically optimal cutoff has not yet been derived.
